summary: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a field of AI that enables computers to work with human language. Common applications include translation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, summarization, and text classification.

Text preprocessing prepares raw language for analysis. Typical steps include tokenization, normalization, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming, and lemmatization. The steps chosen depend on the downstream task.
Bag of Words (BoW) represents a document by counting vocabulary terms. It is simple and useful for baseline classifiers, but it ignores word order and most context.

Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) assigns larger weights to terms that occur frequently in a document but are relatively rare across documents. It is often used for search, document comparison, and text classification.

Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors. In text retrieval, a larger cosine similarity usually means that a query and document share a more similar TF-IDF representation.

Word embeddings map words or tokens to dense numerical vectors. Word2Vec and GloVe learn static representations, while contextual models such as BERT produce representations that depend on surrounding words.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequences by updating a hidden state over time. They can model text sequences but often struggle to preserve information across long distances because of vanishing or exploding gradients.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) are gated RNN architectures. Their gates help control what information is kept or forgotten, improving the modeling of longer dependencies.

Sequence-to-sequence models transform an input sequence into an output sequence. Encoder-decoder models are widely used for machine translation, text summarization, and other generation tasks, often with an attention mechanism.

Attention allows a model to focus on relevant tokens when producing a representation or prediction. Self-attention computes relationships among positions within the same sequence and is a central component of transformers.

Transformers use attention mechanisms and feed-forward layers to model sequences without recurrence. Their architecture supports parallel processing during training and underlies modern models such as BERT, BART, and GPT.

BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is an encoder-only transformer pretrained with masked language modeling. It uses bidirectional context and is commonly fine-tuned for classification, named entity recognition, and question answering.

BART is an encoder-decoder transformer trained to reconstruct corrupted text. It combines a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder and is useful for summarization, generation, and text correction.

Large language models (LLMs) are pretrained on large text corpora to predict or generate tokens. They can answer questions, summarize, and generate text; their responses may still be inaccurate without suitable context or verification.
Named Entity Recognition (NER) identifies and categorizes mentions such as people, organizations, locations, and dates in text. It is a token-level information extraction task.
Sentiment analysis estimates whether text expresses positive, negative, or neutral sentiment. Common approaches include TF-IDF-based classifiers and fine-tuned transformer models.

NLP evaluation depends on the task. Accuracy and F1 are common for classification; precision and recall help with information extraction; BLEU and ROUGE are reference-based metrics for translation and summarization, with important limitations.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant knowledge before asking an LLM to answer. A retriever scores documents against the question, selects useful passages, and supplies them as context so answers can be grounded in the knowledge base.
